content.text: {"relation":"MATCH","consensus_summary":"Babel/Babylon is the archetypal symbol of human pride and self-exaltation — humanity's attempt to make a name for itself and reach heaven by its own power — extended into the image of an idolatrous, oppressive world empire ('the city of man' / anti-God world system) that stands in deliberate contrast to God's city and kingdom and is destined for divine judgment. Disagreements in the tradition concern only the concrete referent of Babylon in Revelation (Rome, papacy, apostate Jerusalem, end-time system, literal rebuilt city), not the core symbolic valence.","book_summary":"Babel/Babylon is 'the self-made kingdom that builds a name against heaven — an empire raised over many kingdoms, the covenant counterfeit': a humanly constructed kingdom of self-exaltation, functioning as an imperial power over the nations and as the counterfeit rival to God's covenant kingdom.","consensus_core_identification":"Human pride and self-made rebellion against God, embodied as the idolatrous world empire/system opposed to God's kingdom and city, doomed to fall.","book_core_identification":"The self-made, name-building kingdom raised against heaven; an empire over many kingdoms that counterfeits God's covenant kingdom.","core_relation":"EQUIVALENT","extension_relation":"SAME_CASES","boundary_disagreement":"None of substance. The book's phrase 'covenant counterfeit' gives a slightly more specific theological framing (Babylon as a parody of God's covenant kingdom), but this is functionally the same as the consensus's 'city of man' set in deliberate contrast to the city of God / New Jerusalem, and does not add or exclude cases.","material_contradiction":"None. Both readings identify Babel/Babylon as prideful, self-exalting human empire opposed to God and destined for judgment.","rationale":"Reduced to minimum cores, both readings say the same thing: a self-made kingdom exalting its own name against God (Gen 11:4), functioning as an empire over the nations (Jer 51:7), opposed to and counterfeiting God's kingdom, and falling under judgment (Rev 18:10). The consensus explicitly includes the counter-image element (Babylon vs. New Jerusalem, city of man vs. city of God), so 'covenant counterfeit' is a wording-level intensification of an idea already present, not a boundary change. The book takes no position on the disputed Revelation referents, so it neither narrows nor broadens the consensus extension.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue for REFINED because 'the covenant counterfeit' asserts a specific structural claim — that Babylon is a deliberate parody of God's covenant order — which is stronger than the consensus's generic 'anti-God world system,' and none of the three printed citations directly establishes covenantal counterfeiting. However, since the Augustinian two-cities contrast is squarely within the consensus, this remains framing rather than a change of referent or extension.","confidence":"high"}
